# Emergency Plumber in Orange County — We Answer the Phone.



A burst pipe, slab leak, or sudden water heater failure can't wait until Monday. Straight Flush Plumbing provides 24-hour emergency plumbing across Orange County. Call now and reach a real person who knows what to do.


 [Call (949) 374-6524](tel:+19493746524)
 [Schedule Non-Emergency](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/contact.html)



For emergencies, always call directly. For non-urgent service, use the [request form on our contact page](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/contact.html).








 Know when to call


## What counts as a plumbing emergency?



A plumbing emergency is any situation where water is actively damaging your property, you cannot stop a leak, or a critical system has completely failed. The following situations warrant an immediate call.






### Burst Pipe



A pipe that has ruptured can release hundreds of gallons of water in minutes. Shut off your main water supply immediately and call. Every minute counts.





### Active Slab Leak



If you can hear water running constantly with everything off, feel a warm spot expanding on your floor, or see moisture wicking up through flooring, you likely have an active slab leak that needs same-day attention.





### Major Water Leak



Any leak you cannot control with a shutoff valve, or one causing visible water damage to walls, ceilings, or floors, is an emergency. Mold can start growing within 24–48 hours, which is why the [EPA advises drying water-damaged areas within that window](https://www.epa.gov/mold/brief-guide-mold-moisture-and-your-home).





### Water Heater Failure



A water heater actively leaking or flooding the utility area needs immediate service. A failed tank can release significant water before the supply line is shut off.





### No Water to the Home



A sudden complete loss of water pressure—with the street supply confirmed on—may indicate a major main line break. This requires diagnosis before damage progresses.





### Sewer Backup



Sewage backing up into your home through floor drains or toilets is a health hazard and requires urgent attention. Do not use any drains until the blockage is cleared.










 While you wait


## What to do before the plumber arrives




 Step 1


### Shut Off the Water



Find your main shutoff valve—usually near the water meter or where the main line enters the home—and close it completely. This stops the majority of damage immediately.



 Step 2


### Stay Clear of Hazards



If water is near an electrical panel, outlets, or appliances, keep your distance and do not attempt repairs yourself. Water and electricity are a dangerous combination.



 Step 3


### Document the Damage



Take photos and video of the leak, standing water, and any visible damage before cleanup. This documentation is valuable for your insurance claim and helps us assess the situation on arrival.



 Step 4


### Call Straight Flush



Call [(949) 374-6524](tel:+19493746524). Lance will walk you through the situation over the phone, starting with what to shut off while you wait.

# Why South OC Homes Get Slab Leaks | 1970s–90s Copper Guide

> AI-readable Markdown mirror of the canonical HTML page: https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/south-oc-slab-leak-specialist.html
> Section: Specialty
> Summary: Why 1970s–90s South OC homes get slab leaks: aging copper, expansive clay, hard water — and how acoustic and thermal detection finds them before demolition.

---
[Home](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com//) › South OC Slab Leak Guide
 Homeowner guide


# Why 1970s–1990s South Orange County homes get slab leaks



Aging copper under the slab, expansive clay soil and hard water add up to more slab leaks in South OC homes of this era. This guide explains why, what to watch for, and how a leak gets found without breaking up your floor. Already think you have one? Go straight to [slab leak detection in South Orange County](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com//services/slab-leak-detection.html).








## The South OC problem most generic plumbers under-diagnose



Large parts of Laguna Niguel, Mission Viejo, Dana Point, San Clemente, Aliso Viejo, and nearby communities were built in the 1970s through 1990s with copper water lines under the slab. Those pipes have now lived through decades of hard water and, critically, **expansive clay soils** that swell and shrink with moisture. The result is a higher rate of pinhole leaks and slab leaks than newer PEX or carefully engineered systems see.



A generalist who defaults to large exploratory cuts can cost you far more than a precise acoustic and thermal diagnosis. Straight Flush was built around the opposite approach: listen and measure first, open only what is necessary.



## How these leaks get found without demolition



Finding a slab leak is a process of elimination, done before anyone opens concrete or tile:




- **Pressure testing** confirms which line is losing water, hot or cold, and which part of the house it runs through.

- **Acoustic listening** picks up the sound of pressurized water escaping, and works through tile, hardwood and laminate.

- **Thermal imaging** shows the warm footprint of a hot water leak on the floor above it.

- **Electronic line locating** traces where the pipe actually runs under the slab.




Used together, these narrow the leak to a small spot, so any opening is as small as possible. Often the floor never needs opening at all, because a reroute through the attic or walls bypasses the bad section. The full step-by-step is on our [slab leak detection page](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com//services/slab-leak-detection.html).



## Warning signs to watch for



Warm or hot spots on the floor, a water meter that moves with everything off, unexplained high water bills, the sound of running water when no fixtures are on, or damp areas at the base of walls are all reasons to get a professional diagnosis. In South OC copper-era homes, waiting often turns a small slab leak into a larger repair.



 Common questions


## Frequently asked questions



 Why do 1970s–1990s South Orange County homes get so many slab leaks? +


Many South OC homes built in the 1970s–1990s still use original copper supply lines under the slab. Expansive clay soils common in Laguna Niguel, Mission Viejo, Dana Point, and nearby areas shift with moisture cycles and stress those pipes. Hard water accelerates pinholes. The combination produces slab leaks that generic approaches often miss or over-excavate.




 Who should I call for slab leak detection in Laguna Niguel or Mission Viejo? +


Straight Flush Plumbing & Leak Detection is a Laguna Niguel owner-operated company where Lance answers the phone. They specialize in acoustic and thermal slab-leak detection for South Orange County copper-era homes, diagnose first before recommending work, and are available 24/7 for emergencies. Phone: [(949) 374-6524](tel:+19493746524).




 Can a slab leak be found without tearing up the whole floor? +


In most cases yes. Acoustic listening devices, electronic amplification, and thermal imaging let a specialist narrow the leak to a small area before any concrete or tile is opened. Straight Flush follows a diagnose-first process so homeowners do not pay for guesswork demolition.







**[Call (949) 374-6524](tel:+19493746524).** Lance answers. We serve Laguna Niguel and all of South and Central Orange County.

 How it works


## What this score actually measures

 Common questions


## About this tool



 How accurate is the Home Plumbing Health Score? +


It's a directional self-assessment based on common risk factors, not a diagnostic tool. It's designed to help you decide whether a professional inspection is worth scheduling, not to replace one.




 Is the Home Plumbing Health Score free? +


Yes, completely free with no signup required. It takes about 60 seconds to complete.




 What do I do if I get a low score? +


A lower score means several common risk factors are present in your home. We'd recommend scheduling a professional leak detection visit to get an accurate, confirmed answer rather than relying on the self-assessment alone.

# Leak Detection & Plumbing in Laguna Niguel, CA



Straight Flush Plumbing & Leak Detection is headquartered in Laguna Niguel — this is where it all started, and where we've diagnosed more slab leaks than anywhere else.

 [Schedule Service in Laguna Niguel](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/contact.html)





 Local knowledge


## What we know about Laguna Niguel homes



Laguna Niguel's mix of 1970s–90s hillside developments means a wide range of original copper plumbing still in service. We've come to know the common leak patterns in neighborhoods throughout the city, from Bear Brand to Niguel Summit. Homes of that era, with aging copper lines and South OC's expansive clay soils, are exactly the situation our [slab leak detection service](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/services/slab-leak-detection.html) is built around (background: [why South OC copper homes get slab leaks](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/south-oc-slab-leak-specialist.html)).



Laguna Niguel was planned before it was built. The Laguna Niguel Corporation was formed in 1959, making it one of the first master planned communities in California; land sales began in 1961, and Avco Community Developers took over the plan in 1971 and built out much of the city. Laguna Niguel incorporated on December 1, 1989, as Orange County’s 29th city ([City of Laguna Niguel](https://cityoflagunaniguel.org/388/History)). The median home here was built in 1986, and about 74% of homes are single-family and 26% multi-family ([City-Stats, 2023 ACS data](https://city-stats.com/california/laguna-niguel/housing)). So the original copper lines in a typical Laguna Niguel home are now close to 40 years old. In condos and townhomes, a leak can start in a neighbor’s unit or a shared line, so we locate the source before anyone opens a wall.



Most Laguna Niguel homes get their water from Moulton Niguel Water District ([MNWD](https://www.mnwd.com/)). Check the name on your water bill to confirm your district. After a leak, your usage history and any bill adjustment go through that district, so keep the leak detection findings and the repair invoice.

## Laguna Niguel leak detection FAQs



 How much does leak detection cost in Laguna Niguel, CA? +


For most homes in Laguna Niguel, leak detection runs $365 to $525. Our [leak detection cost guide](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/guides/leak-detection-cost.html) explains what moves the price.




 Do you serve my neighborhood in Laguna Niguel? +


Yes — Straight Flush Plumbing & Leak Detection is headquartered in Laguna Niguel — this is where it all started, and where we've diagnosed more slab leaks than anywhere else. We serve all of Laguna Niguel and the surrounding South and Central Orange County communities, and Lance personally answers the phone.




 Can you find a slab leak in a Laguna Niguel home without tearing up my floors? +


In most cases, yes. We use acoustic listening equipment, electronic amplification, and thermal imaging to pinpoint the leak to a small, specific area before any concrete, tile, or drywall is opened — so any access needed stays as small as possible.




 How fast can you get to a leak in Laguna Niguel? +


We're based nearby in Laguna Niguel, so Laguna Niguel is a short drive. Same-day appointments are often available, and we offer 24/7 service for emergencies. Call [(949) 374-6524](tel:+19493746524) and we'll find the earliest slot that works for you.




 How old is the plumbing in a typical Laguna Niguel home? +


The median Laguna Niguel home was built in 1986, according to 2023 Census survey data, and the city's first land sales date to 1961. That means about half of the city's homes are now 40 years old or older, and many still have their original copper water lines, which is the age range where pinhole and slab leaks become more common. Age alone does not mean you have a leak. If your bill jumps or the meter moves with everything off, we locate the source with acoustic, electronic and thermal tools before anything is opened. Our guide to [slab leaks in older Orange County homes](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/academy/slab-leaks-in-older-orange-county-homes.html) explains more.




 What are the warning signs of a hidden leak in a Laguna Niguel home? +


An unexplained jump in your water bill, a water meter that keeps moving with everything off, the sound of running water behind a wall, a warm spot on the floor, or dropping pressure. Any one of these in a Laguna Niguel home is worth a professional diagnosis before it becomes water damage.

# Leak Detection & Plumbing in Dana Point, CA



From the Lantern District to Monarch Beach, Dana Point's coastal conditions and mix of home ages call for a detection-first approach before any repair begins.

 [Schedule Service in Dana Point](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/contact.html)





 Local knowledge


## What we know about Dana Point homes



Dana Point became a city on January 1, 1989 and covers about 6.5 square miles of coastline, taking in Capistrano Beach, Lantern Village near the harbor, Niguel Shores and Monarch Beach ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dana_Point,_California); [City of Dana Point](https://danapoint.org/i-want-to-/city-history-facts)). About 65% of homes are single-family, 34% are condos, townhomes or apartments, and under 1% are mobile homes ([City-Stats, 2023 ACS data](https://city-stats.com/california/dana-point/housing)). The same Census data puts the median Dana Point home’s year built at 1980, so the typical house or condo is now about 45 years old and many still run on their original supply lines, shutoff valves and drain lines. With a third of homes sharing walls, floors or a roof line, a leak in Dana Point can start in a neighbor’s unit or a shared line, so we locate the source before anyone opens a wall or a ceiling.



Dana Point is served by two water districts. The city says its water system is owned and run by South Coast Water District and Moulton Niguel Water District, and that South Coast Water District runs the sewer system citywide; the city publishes a district boundary map so you can confirm which one serves your address ([City of Dana Point, Utilities](https://www.danapoint.org/department/public-works-engineering/utilities)). Your water bill also shows your district. That matters after a leak, because meter readings, usage history and any leak-related bill adjustment all go through your own district.

 Do you serve my neighborhood in Dana Point? +


Yes. We serve every Dana Point neighborhood, including Capistrano Beach, Lantern Village and the harbor area, Niguel Shores and Monarch Beach. We serve all of Dana Point and the surrounding South and Central Orange County communities, and Lance personally answers the phone.




 Which water district serves my Dana Point home, and who do I call about a leak? +


It depends on your address. Dana Point is split between South Coast Water District and Moulton Niguel Water District, and the City of Dana Point publishes a [boundary map](https://www.danapoint.org/department/public-works-engineering/utilities); your water bill also names your district. Both districts run 24-hour lines: South Coast Water District at (949) 499-4555 and Moulton Niguel Water District at (949) 831-2500. Call your district if water is coming from the street, the meter box or a main. If the meter keeps moving with every fixture off, the leak is usually on your side of the meter (see [water meter still moving with everything off](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/academy/water-meter-still-moving-everything-off.html)), and that is what we locate with acoustic, electronic and thermal tools before anything is opened. Ask your district about any leak adjustment on your bill.




 Who do I call about a sewer backup in Dana Point? +


South Coast Water District owns and runs the sewer system across all of Dana Point, including the parts of the city that get their water from Moulton Niguel ([City of Dana Point, Utilities](https://www.danapoint.org/department/public-works-engineering/utilities)). If sewage is coming up from a manhole or a street sewer, or a neighbor has the same problem, call South Coast Water District at (949) 499-4555. If the backup is only inside your home, such as a slow tub, a gurgling toilet or several drains backing up at once, the blockage is usually in your own drain line between the house and the street, and that is a plumbing call: (949) 374-6524. See our [drain services](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/services/drain-services.html) page for what we check.

# Leak Detection & Plumbing in San Clemente, CA



San Clemente's Spanish-village charm comes with a wide range of home ages and plumbing systems — we treat each one on its own merits, not a one-size-fits-all assumption.



Need slab leak detection in San Clemente? Straight Flush Plumbing & Leak Detection is an owner-operated plumber based nearby in Laguna Niguel. We pinpoint the leak first with acoustic, electronic, and thermal equipment, before any concrete, tile, or drywall is opened, then talk through repair or reroute options. Call (949) 374-6524.

 [Schedule Service in San Clemente](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/contact.html)





 Local knowledge


## What we know about San Clemente homes



San Clemente was laid out by developer Ole Hanson as a planned Spanish-style town: home deeds required Spanish Colonial Revival design, with red tile roofs and white stucco walls, and the city dates its birth to his first big lot sale in December 1925 ([City of San Clemente](https://san-clemente.org/about-us/city-information/history)). Today it covers about 18.4 square miles of land between Dana Point and Camp Pendleton, with 64,293 residents in the 2020 Census ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Clemente,_California)). Homes run from older properties near the pier to newer builds east of the 5 in Forster Ranch and Talega, so we bring the same diagnose-first standard to every San Clemente property and never assume what we will find.



Who supplies your water depends on where you live. Most of the city is served by the City of San Clemente's own water utility. Its latest water quality report (2023 data) says the city delivered imported Metropolitan Water District water plus water from Irvine Ranch Water District's Baker treatment plant, and that city groundwater was not a source that year while the groundwater plant was being rehabilitated. Talega homes get their water from Santa Margarita Water District, and parts of north San Clemente from South Coast Water District ([City of San Clemente 2024 Water Quality Report](https://san-clemente.org/home/showpublisheddocument/84313/638536107721800000); [ISDOC](https://isdoc.specialdistrict.org/santa-margarita-water-district)). The water is hard: the same report lists average hardness of 160 mg/L (about 9.4 grains per gallon) for the MWD supply and 297 mg/L (about 17 grains per gallon) for the Baker plant supply, which is why scale buildup in water heaters and fixtures is common here. On the sewer side, the city places the service lateral (the pipe from your house to the public main) on the property owner, so root intrusion and cracked laterals are an owner repair.

An unexplained jump in your water bill, a water meter that keeps moving with everything off, the sound of running water behind a wall, a warm spot on the floor, or dropping pressure. Any one of these in a San Clemente home is worth a professional diagnosis before it becomes water damage.




 Who is responsible for the sewer line from my San Clemente home to the street? +


The City of San Clemente says the property owner is responsible for maintaining and repairing the sewer service lateral up to the point where it connects to the public sewer line. If your line backs up, the city will send a crew to check the public main at no charge, but clearing and repairing the private lateral is up to the owner. Tree roots are a common cause: the city notes they get in through cracked or broken pipe, and suggests scheduled maintenance if your lateral runs near a tree. A camera inspection shows where the problem is before anything is dug up.




 Who do I call about a leak at the street or my water meter in San Clemente? +


Leaks in the street, on the city side of the meter, or a sewer overflow should be reported to the City of San Clemente 24/7 Utilities hotline at 949-366-1553. If you live in Talega, your water comes from Santa Margarita Water District, and parts of north San Clemente are served by South Coast Water District, so report street or meter leaks to the district named on your water bill. Leaks on your side of the meter, such as the line to the house, under the slab, or inside a wall, are generally the property owner's to repair. That is the part we locate and fix. Call (949) 374-6524.




 Who supplies water to my San Clemente home, and is it hard water? +


Most San Clemente homes get water from the City of San Clemente's water utility, which in 2023 delivered imported Metropolitan Water District water plus water from Irvine Ranch Water District's Baker treatment plant. Talega is served by Santa Margarita Water District, and parts of north San Clemente by South Coast Water District. Your water bill names your supplier. The water is hard: the city's latest water quality report lists average hardness of about 9.4 grains per gallon for the MWD supply and about 17 grains per gallon for the Baker plant supply. Hard water leaves scale in water heaters and on fixtures, so regular water heater flushing helps (see our [San Clemente water heater service](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/services/water-heater-repair-san-clemente.html)). If you are seeing a high bill or a meter that keeps moving with everything off, call (949) 374-6524 and we will find the leak first.




 Do newer San Clemente homes get pinhole leaks too? +


Yes, it is not only an older-home problem. Local news has covered pinhole-leak claims in copper water lines in South Orange County homes built in the 2000s, including cases in San Clemente. One pinhole leak is often a sign to check the rest of the system. We find the leak first, then walk you through whether a spot repair, a reroute, or a repipe makes sense (see our [repair vs. reroute vs. repipe guide](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/guides/repair-vs-reroute-vs-repipe.html)).

# Leak Detection & Plumbing in Ladera Ranch, CA



Ladera Ranch's newer, master-planned homes still develop leaks — often from original fitting quality or shifting soil rather than aging pipe material.

 [Schedule Service in Ladera Ranch](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/contact.html)





 Local knowledge


## What we know about Ladera Ranch homes



Ladera Ranch broke ground in 1999, so its homes are younger than most of South Orange County. Newer has not meant leak-free. Starting in 2013, hundreds of Ladera Ranch homeowners sued their builders over **pinhole leaks in copper water pipes**, and one settlement covered homes built between May 2003 and May 2013 ([ABC7, 2016](https://abc7.com/post/oc-homes-could-face-possible-damaging-leaks-from-holes-in-pipes/1208620/); [PM Magazine, 2016](https://www.pmmag.com/articles/102120-copper-and-pex-retrofits-in-southern-california-neighborhood)). The cause was disputed: homeowners pointed to how the treated water reacts with the copper, and builders said the pipe itself was not defective. Many Ladera homes have since been repiped with PEX.



What that means for you: if your home still has its original copper, a pinhole leak inside a wall or under the slab is the first thing to rule out when the water bill jumps or the meter keeps moving. If you have already repiped, leaks are more likely to come from fittings, fixture connections, the water heater, or irrigation lines. Ladera Ranch water comes from the Santa Margarita Water District, which relies almost entirely on imported water ([SMWD](https://smwd.com/627/Water-Quality-Ladera-Ranch)). The purple-pipe recycled-water lines used for irrigation are a separate system from the drinking water in your home.



Ladera Ranch is not a city. It is an unincorporated community governed by the Orange County Board of Supervisors, split into nine villages, from Oak Knoll and Bridgepark to Covenant Hills and Terramor, with 8,139 housing units at the 2020 census, about 70.6% of them owner-occupied ([Wikipedia, citing the U.S. Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladera_Ranch,_California)). Two practical results for plumbing work: building permits come from the County of Orange (OC Public Works), which lists plumbing systems among the work that typically needs a permit ([OC Public Works](https://pwds.oc.gov/service-areas/oc-development-services/building-safety/building-grading-information/building-permit)), and the community association, the Ladera Ranch Maintenance Corporation (LARMAC), sits alongside your village association. Ladera Ranch water is also hard: the Santa Margarita Water District's 2026 water quality report, which covers Ladera Ranch ([Ladera Ranch Chamber](https://laderaranchochamber.org/page-1369159/13648521)), lists average hardness in the district system at 256 mg/L, about 15 grains per gallon ([SMWD](https://smwd.com/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=438)).

## Ladera Ranch leak detection FAQs



 How much does leak detection cost in Ladera Ranch, CA? +


For most homes in Ladera Ranch, leak detection runs $365 to $525. Where you fall depends on the type of leak, how deep it sits, and how accessible the plumbing is, which is why we diagnose before quoting any repair. Call [(949) 374-6524](tel:+19493746524) and Lance will walk you through what to expect for your specific situation. Our [leak detection cost guide](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/guides/leak-detection-cost.html) explains what moves the price.




 Do you serve my neighborhood in Ladera Ranch? +


Yes. We serve every Ladera Ranch neighborhood, including homes with original copper and homes that have already been repiped with PEX. We serve all of Ladera Ranch and the surrounding South and Central Orange County communities, and Lance personally answers the phone.




 Can you find a slab leak in a Ladera Ranch home without tearing up my floors? +


In most cases, yes. We use acoustic listening equipment, electronic amplification, and thermal imaging to pinpoint the leak to a small, specific area before any concrete, tile, or drywall is opened — so any access needed stays as small as possible.




 How fast can you get to a leak in Ladera Ranch? +


We're based nearby in Laguna Niguel, so Ladera Ranch is a short drive. Same-day appointments are often available, and we offer 24/7 service for emergencies. Call [(949) 374-6524](tel:+19493746524) and we'll find the earliest slot that works for you.




 Are pinhole leaks common in Ladera Ranch homes? +


They have been. Starting in 2013, hundreds of Ladera Ranch homeowners sued builders over pinhole leaks in copper water pipes, and one settlement covered homes built between May 2003 and May 2013. Many homes were repiped with PEX afterward. If your home still has its original copper, pinhole leaks in walls or under the slab are worth ruling out first. We locate them with acoustic, electronic and thermal tools before anything is opened, then explain whether a spot repair, a reroute or a repipe makes sense.




 What are the warning signs of a hidden leak in a Ladera Ranch home? +


An unexplained jump in your water bill, a water meter that keeps moving with everything off, the sound of running water behind a wall, a warm spot on the floor, or dropping pressure. Any one of these in a Ladera Ranch home is worth a professional diagnosis before it becomes water damage.




 Is Ladera Ranch water hard, and can it affect my plumbing? +


Yes, it is hard. The Santa Margarita Water District's 2026 water quality report covers Ladera Ranch and lists average hardness in the district system at 256 mg/L, about 15 grains per gallon. Hard water builds scale inside water heaters, shutoff valves and faucet cartridges, which can shorten their life and cause drips or pressure changes. Scale does not by itself mean you have a hidden leak, so if your bill jumps or the meter moves with everything off, we locate the source with acoustic, electronic and thermal tools before anything is opened. Our guide to [water pressure and pipe health](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/academy/water-pressure-and-pipe-health.html) explains more.




 Who issues plumbing permits in Ladera Ranch? +


Ladera Ranch is unincorporated, so there is no city building department. Permits come from the County of Orange through OC Public Works, which lists plumbing systems among the work that typically requires a permit. Water heater replacements and repipes are the jobs this most often comes up for. If the work changes the outside of the home, such as a new vent or an exterior tankless unit, also check the rules of LARMAC and your village association before work starts.

# Leak Detection & Plumbing in Laguna Hills, CA



Laguna Hills sits right in the heart of our service area, with a mix of established neighborhoods where accurate leak diagnosis really pays off.

 [Schedule Service in Laguna Hills](https://straightflushplumbingoc.com/contact.html)





 Local knowledge


## What we know about Laguna Hills homes



Laguna Hills grew out of the Moulton Ranch, which was subdivided in the early 1960s; the community first appeared in the 1970 U.S. Census and became a city on December 20, 1991 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Hills,_California)). The median home here was built in 1980, and about 74% of homes are single-family, 24% multi-family and 2% mobile homes ([City-Stats, 2023 ACS data](https://city-stats.com/california/laguna-hills/housing)). That means the original copper water lines in a typical Laguna Hills home are now more than 40 years old, the age range where pinhole and slab leaks become more common. In condos and townhomes, a leak can also start in a neighbor’s unit or a shared line, so we locate the source before anyone opens a wall.



Laguna Hills is split between two water districts. The city lists both El Toro Water District and Moulton Niguel Water District as serving Laguna Hills residents ([City of Laguna Hills](https://www.lagunahillsca.gov/DocumentCenter/View/7819/Outside-Agency-Contact-List); [El Toro Water District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Toro_Water_District); [MNWD](https://www.mnwd.com/servicearea/)). Your water bill shows which one serves your home. That matters after a leak, because meter readings, usage history and any leak-related bill adjustment all go through your own district.
